html:
The Battle of Rossbach was fought on 5 November 1757 near the village of Rossbach in Saxony, in today's eastern Germany. Frederick the Great of Prussia, with about 22,000 men, routed a French and German imperial army of about 41,000.

It was the second year of the Seven Years' War. Prussia was surrounded by enemies: Austria, France, Russia and Sweden. A French army under the Prince of Soubise, joined by troops of the Holy Roman Empire, marched into Saxony. They tried to swing round Frederick's left side and cut him off. Frederick pretended to retreat, then moved his army quickly behind a low hill. His cavalry under General Seydlitz charged the heads of the marching columns before they could form up, and his guns and infantry finished the work. The fighting lasted about ninety minutes. The allies lost about 10,000 men, half of them prisoners. Prussia lost about 550.

France never again sent an army against Frederick himself, and Britain raised its payments to Prussia. Frederick was free to march east to Silesia, where he won at Leuthen a month later. Rossbach also became a source of pride across the German lands.
